extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, journalists, and policymakers interested in disinformation and information integrity
extracted.subtask_description: A broad, encyclopedic summary of disinformation: definitions, purposes, mechanisms, tactics, amplification channels (especially online advertising and computational propaganda), and methods to counter it. Intended as a reference/overview rather than a prescriptive how-to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four main methods of seeding disinformation online
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies show four main methods of seeding disinformation online: Selective censorship; Manipulation of search rankings; Hacking and releasing; Directly sharing disinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This enumeration identifies the primary operational vectors through which disinformation is introduced and propagated on the internet. (Original phrasing: 'Studies show four main methods of seeding disinformation online: Selective censorship; Manipulation of search rankings; Hacking and releasing; Directly sharing disinformation.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposes of internet manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Internet manipulation may be used to steer public opinion, polarise citizens, circulate conspiracy theories, and silence political dissidents. It can also be done for profit (e.g., to harm corporate or political adversaries and improve brand reputation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identifies the motivations that disinformation campaigns serve — political influence, social polarization, reputational/financial gain, and censorship or selective enforcement (including selective violations of net neutrality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Computational propaganda (definition / category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Internet manipulation for propaganda purposes with the help of data analysis and internet bots in social media is called computational propaganda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labels a class of disinformation that combines automated accounts, data-driven targeting, and programmatic amplification to influence public debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI swarms as an emergent threat
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns that AI technology could enable groups of AI programs, known as 'AI swarms,' to autonomously coordinate to manipulate democratic discourse by maintaining persistent fake identities and mimicking human social dynamics over extended periods of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights an emergent capability/risk dimension: autonomous coordination of many AI agents that can sustain long-running deceptive interactions and identity persistence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploiting online advertising technologies to amplify disinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Disinformation is amplified online due to malpractice concerning online advertising, especially the machine-to-machine interactions of real-time bidding systems. Online advertising technologies have been used to amplify disinformation due to the financial incentives and monetization of user-generated content and fake news. The lax oversight over the online advertising market can be used to amplify disinformation, including the use of dark money used for political advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identifies the economic/technical amplification channel: programmatic advertising (real-time bidding, automated ad tech) and monetization dynamics, plus regulatory/oversight weaknesses that enable campaign funding and distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological mechanisms that enable disinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychological-level mechanisms listed include cognitive bias, the misinformation effect, denialism and other psychological vulnerabilities that facilitate acceptance and spread of false information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are human-cognition and social-psychology vectors that make audiences susceptible to disinformation (e.g., echo chambers, motivated reasoning). They are presented as core mechanisms by which disinformation spreads and persists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computational mechanisms that enable disinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Computational mechanisms include algorithmic radicalization, content moderation (and its failures), community notes, internet manipulation techniques, social bots, and the role of social networking services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are platform-level, algorithmic, and automation factors that shape exposure and amplification (recommendation systems, botnets, automated posting, moderation policies and enforcement gaps).

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic mechanisms that enable disinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic/systemic mechanisms include fake news websites, surveillance capitalism, programmatic advertising, audience fragmentation, monetization incentives, and broader media-economics drivers that make disinformation profitable and scalable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames disinformation as a market-shaped phenomenon: monetization and advertising ecosystems create incentives for producing and amplifying deceptive content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda techniques and tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: A long list of propaganda techniques and deceptive tactics used in disinformation campaigns: astroturfing, accusation in a mirror, ad hominem, appeal to fear, appeal to emotion, atrocity propaganda, bandwagon effect, big lie, black propaganda, cherry picking, circular reporting, clickbait, conspiracy theory, doublespeak, gaslighting, forgeries, false balance, fear-uncertainty-and-doubt, firehose of falsehood, dog whistle, smear campaigns, and many others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This catalogue functions as a taxonomy of specific tactics used to construct and distribute deceptive narratives. Recognizing these techniques helps in classifying and countering instances of disinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods to counter disinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Countering approaches and interventions mentioned include academic research, critical thinking, digital literacy, health literacy, information literacy, media literacy, science communication, scientific consensus messaging, scientific literacy, truth sandwich, Verificado-style verification, watchdog journalism, and fact-checking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This groups educational, research, journalistic, and communicative interventions aimed at mitigation and resilience. The article also lists non-profits, fact-checking organizations, and resources (e.g., Africa Check, FactCheck.org, Full Fact, PolitiFact, NewsGuard) as practical countermeasures and actors.
